entities.name: Jorge da Costa
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dom Jorge da Costa (c. 1406–1508), known as the 'Cardinal of Alpedrinha' or 'Cardinal of Lisbon,' was a Portuguese cardinal and statesman whose lengthy career spanned the tumultuous late 15th and early 16th centuries, a period marked by papal intrigue, the rise of powerful European monarchies, and the burgeoning Age of Discovery. Serving under five popes—Sixtus IV, Innocent VIII, Alexander VI, Pius III, and Julius II—da Costa leveraged his considerable diplomatic acumen and vast personal wealth to become a central, albeit often controversial, figure in the Roman Curia and a significant arbiter of Portuguese-papal relations.

Elevated to Cardinal-Priest in 1476 by Sixtus IV, da Costa's influence grew through key appointments, including Archbishop of Lisbon (1464-1500) and various other dioceses across Portugal, Italy, and Spain. He actively participated in several papal conclaves, most notably the contentious 1492 election that saw Rodrigo Borgia ascend to the papacy as Alexander VI. Da Costa was a prominent patron of arts and letters, commissioning works and endowing institutions, reflecting the Renaissance ideal of the cardinal-prince. His involvement in the political machinations of the Vatican often saw him at odds with rival factions, yet his resilience and strategic alliances ensured his enduring power and wealth, which he often directed towards Portuguese interests and the expansion of the Portuguese overseas empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jorge da Costa was a pivotal figure in late 15th-century European diplomacy, influencing papal-Portuguese relations and the early Age of Discovery. His extensive patronage also left a lasting mark on Portuguese religious and cultural institutions.
